items.title: Everyone is a scalability expert till traffic spikes
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Once upon a time, there lived a junior software engineer named Michiko.

She worked for a tech company named Hooli.

Although she was bright, she never got promoted.

So she was sad & frustrated…

Until one day, she had the idea to apply for a new job.

And the interviewer asked her 1 simple question:

“How to effectively scale a system?”

But she couldn’t answer it & failed the interview in 5 minutes.

So she went home & studied it to fill the knowledge gap.

Your coding agent can already paste a Mermaid chart into a PR description.

You still read every file to learn what it does to your system.

draws each pull request as a live architecture canvas, right in your pull request. Press play and it walks you through the change, one step at a time.

  • , marked on the parts of the system it touches

  • , including services the diff never names

  • through the system now

  • , flagged before you merge

2,200+ GitHub stars and 45,000+ pull requests drawn.

(Thanks to Coldtea for partnering on this newsletter.)

Michiko failed the interview, so you don’t have to.

And here are 11 must-know scalability techniques for you to ace job interviews:

Vertical scaling gives one machine more power by adding CPU, memory, and/or faster disks.

The app stays the same, but the machine it runs on gets more powerful... Or you move the app to a larger instance.

i.e., you do NOT need to rewrite any code. And vertical scaling is probably the quickest way to handle extra load.

It works well for monoliths & older systems built to run on a machine.

Yet larger machines cost more & all machines have limits.

Plus, if your app relies on a single server, a failure could take the entire app down.

So scale up when you need more capacity quickly. Then consider horizontal scaling before one machine becomes your system’s biggest bottleneck.

Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more machines to share the load.

You run several copies of the app & distribute traffic across them using a load balancer.

i.e., you add machines as traffic grows & remove them when demand drops.

It works well for applications with high/unpredictable traffic.

Yet adding machines creates new challenges:

You need load balancing, coordination between instances & keep shared data consistent.

Horizontal scaling improves “availability” with redundant instances. But if your app stores user sessions locally, requests routed to different instances could lose access to session data.

So before you scale out, you need to decide where your application stores its state.

And that’s why you’d need stateless services...

A stateless service does NOT store client session state between requests.

Every request provides information the server needs - auth token or session ID.

Plus, you don’t store session data on server… instead, you keep it in a shared database, a cache like Redis, or use a signed token like a JSON Web Token ().

i.e., any server could handle a request without relying on the previous one.

This makes it easier to add, remove, or replace servers as traffic patterns change.

Yet the state still needs to live somewhere.

And an external database/cache adds infrastructure, network latency & an extra dependency to manage. Plus, relying on sticky sessions to keep users tied to one server reduces flexibility when servers fail or traffic changes.

So keep session state outside individual app instances when possible. Also, design operations to be “idempotent”.

With stateless services, you could scale individual instances more easily.

But what if those services depend heavily on each other…

That’s where you’d need loose coupling...

Loose coupling = each component depends on others as little as possible.

A change in one component could force you to update several others in a “tightly coupled” system.

Plus, if one service becomes slow/fails, the problem could spread to other services that depend on it.

Loose coupling reduces these dependencies by letting components communicate through well-defined interfaces - APIs/messages. So each component knows what to expect from others without understanding their internal implementation.

This makes it easier to update, deploy, and/or scale components independently.

Yet loose coupling introduces extra complexity:

Requests could travel across many services,,, thus making it HARD to trace & debug failures. Also,splitting a system into many tiny services increases communication overhead & coordination costs.

So use loose coupling when components need to evolve independently - microservices & big apps.

And to organize these components into clear, manageable parts, you need modular architecture…

Modular architecture divides a system into separate modules, with each responsible for a specific function.

You divide the app into modules for authentication, orders, payments, notifications, and so on.

i.e., each module has a clear responsibility & communicates with others through defined interfaces.

The goal is to group functionality that belongs together & keep dependencies between modules . This follows the principle of : each module focuses on one part of the system.

So you update/test payment module without changing the authentication module.

Yet choosing the “wrong module boundaries” creates unnecessary dependencies.

Plus, splitting an app into many modules makes the codebase hard to manage. Also, modules within the same app still share resources & failure risks.

So modularity alone does NOT guarantee independent scaling or failure isolation.

It works well for large applications, modular monoliths & microservice architectures!

But if these modules need to communicate without waiting for each other…you’d need event-driven architecture…

6. Event-driven architecture

Event-driven architecture allows services to communicate by publishing & reacting to events.

A service publishes an event to a message broker instead of calling other services directly.

Imagine a user places an order on an e-commerce website:

The service publishes an event… Then other services consume it independently:

  • service reserves ordered items,

  • service initiates payment processing,

  • service sends an order confirmation when required steps succeed.

service does NOT wait for each consumer to finish processing the event.

i.e., a slow consumer does NOT block others.

This approach works well for workflows when many services need to react to the same event.

Yet event-driven systems create new problems:

Events could arrive late, out of order, or more than once. Plus, different services could temporarily hold different versions of the same data. This is called .

So you need idempotent consumers, reliable event delivery & a way to handle failed operations.

Event-driven architecture helps services scale independently & reduces synchronous dependencies.

But when you need to organize these services without creating a central bottleneck, you’ve got to “avoid” …

7. Shared-nothing architecture

Shared-nothing architecture gives each node its own compute, memory & storage relying on shared resources for processing.

items.title: GitOps Deep Dive: How ArgoCD Works
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
The CI/CD pipeline changed how we deploy software.

It made deployments faster, repeatable, and automated. But once a deployment finishes, the pipeline has no idea what happens inside the cluster afterward.

Someone could edit a Deployment with , apply a hotfix during an incident, or update a resource manually. Those changes bypass Git and the pipeline.

As manual changes increase, the cluster slowly drifts from what gets stored in Git.

At some point, production no longer matches the configuration everyone believes is running. When an issue appears, it becomes difficult to see what changed... Also it becomes difficult to know who changed it or whether the running state still matches the last reviewed configuration.

GitOps solves this by making Git the source of truth for the cluster…not just another step in the deployment process…

An agent continuously compares the live cluster with the desired state stored in Git and reconciles any differences. If someone changes a resource outside Git, ArgoCD detects the drift and brings the cluster back to the expected state.

The CI pipeline still builds, tests, and publishes the application.

But instead of deploying directly to Kubernetes, it updates Git. ArgoCD then handles the deployment and keeps the cluster aligned with the repository.

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

(Thanks to Unblocked for partnering on this newsletter.)

I want to introduce as a guest author.

He’s a Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) who writes about Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, and cloud-native systems. He builds in public and shares practical tips, projects, and lessons learned along the way.

Check out his work & socials:

  • Your deployment succeeds. Then production starts drifting. How manual Kubernetes changes create configuration drift, why traditional CI/CD pipelines miss them, and how GitOps keeps your cluster aligned with Git.

  • Your CI pipeline no longer needs the keys to Kubernetes. How ArgoCD’s pull-based model changes deployments, where credentials live, and what happens when a system gets compromised.

  • ArgoCD runs a reconciliation loop behind the scenes. How its core components detect changes, compare desired and live states, and use sync policies, self-healing, and hooks to control deployments.

  • One template, hundreds of applications. How ApplicationSets manage deployments across clusters, why repository structure matters, and how Git commits promote releases from development to production.

  • GitOps gets harder when you reach production. How to manage secrets, access control, monitoring, progressive delivery, and disaster recovery, plus the tradeoffs you need to understand before adopting it.

GitOps is an operating model where a Git repository is the single source of truth for everything running in your infrastructure.

Every change to your application or cluster configuration happens through a Git commit. It gets reviewed, approved, and merged through the same process as application code.

i.e., changes are not applied directly to the cluster outside Git.

The OpenGitOps working group at CNCF defined four principles to distinguish GitOps from a traditional deployment pipeline.

In a declarative system, you describe what you want, not how to get there.

Instead of writing a script with steps like “create this deployment, then scale it to three replicas, then expose it on port 80,” you write a YAML file describing the end state. The system figures out how to make it happen.

Kubernetes is declarative by nature.

Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and raw YAML manifests all follow the same model.

This matters for GitOps because a declarative system supports storage, versioning, and comparison. Unlike a sequence of commands, two YAML files allow you to see exactly what changed.

2. Versioned and Immutable

Every change to the desired state is a Git commit.

And Git commits do not change…

This gives you a complete, tamper-evident history of everything your cluster has ever been asked to run. Who requested the change, who approved it, when it got merged, and exactly what it modified. The audit trail becomes part of the deployment workflow, not a separate system.

Rollback is also a natural consequence of this principle. Reverting to a previous state means reverting a commit.

This principle changes who is responsible for applying changes.

Instead of an external CI/CD pipeline pushing updates into Kubernetes, an agent inside the cluster pulls the desired state from Git… It then applies the changes.

The security implications of this shift are significant, and they get their own section shortly.

4. Continuously Reconciled

The previous three principles describe how state gets defined and delivered.

This one describes what happens after:

Continuous reconciliation means repeatedly comparing the live cluster state with the desired state in Git. These comparisons detect changes introduced by a manual edit, an autoscaler, or a partial update. The configured sync policy determines whether ArgoCD reports the difference or corrects it automatically.

To understand why GitOps works differently, we first need to compare it with the deployment model most people already use…

CD Without GitOps vs CD With GitOps

With the four principles in place, the difference between traditional CD & GitOps is easier to see.

It is not just a philosophical shift. The two models produce different security properties and failure modes.

They also provide different levels of visibility into what runs in production…

How CD Worked Before GitOps

In a traditional push-based setup, the CI/CD pipeline carries a release from source code to the Kubernetes cluster.

It runs tests, builds a container image, and pushes the image to a registry. The deployment stage then updates Kubernetes using a command such as or .

For example, releasing version 1.5 means the pipeline updates the Deployment to use the new image. Kubernetes then replaces the existing pods according to the configured rollout strategy.

The pipeline directly initiates the deployment. The deployment stage delivers the new configuration to the cluster.

With ArgoCD, the pipeline still tests the application, builds the image, and publishes it to a registry. It then updates the image reference in the configuration repository.

For the same version 1.5 release, the pipeline changes the image tag in a Kubernetes manifest, Helm values file, or Kustomize configuration. This change becomes a Git commit rather than a deployment command executed against the cluster.

ArgoCD detects the updated configuration and compares it with the live resources. With automated sync enabled, it applies the update. With manual sync, it waits for an operator to trigger synchronization. Kubernetes then performs the rollout.

i.e., Git becomes the handoff between the two systems.

CI produces the image and records the intended version. ArgoCD handles applying the configuration to Kubernetes.

This separation also changes where deployment credentials are needed, which brings us to the security boundary between push and pull.

Push vs Pull: Security Boundary

The shift from push to pull is not just an architectural preference.

It changes where credentials live, how far a compromised system can reach, and the damage a supply chain attack can cause.

Now let’s compare the two approaches:

Push-Based: Pipeline Holds the Keys

In a push-based model, the CI pipeline needs direct access to the cluster to deploy anything.

i.e., cluster credentials live inside the CI system.

Anyone with sufficient access to the CI system or pipeline configuration could also gain access to those credentials. Every third-party action, plugin, or integration running inside the pipeline runs adjacent to them. And because pipelines are triggered by code changes, a compromised dependency runs in the pipeline. It runs in the same environment as your cluster credentials.

A compromised pipeline in this model is effectively a compromised cluster.

The attacker does not need to find a vulnerability in Kubernetes… They just need to get malicious code into the build process & let the pipeline do the rest.

The blast radius is as wide as the credentials allow.

For most engineers, those credentials have broad permissions. Restricting them precisely is operationally painful. A compromised push-based pipeline often means cluster-admin access is in the wrong hands.

Pull-Based: Cluster Holds the Keys

In a pull-based model, the cluster reaches out to Git.

The CI system never touches the cluster.

ArgoCD runs inside the cluster with scoped RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) permissions. It pulls the desired state from Git and applies it. The CI pipeline updates the Git repository when a build succeeds, and its job ends there. No cluster credentials ever leave the cluster environment.

A compromised CI system in this model could modify Git.

But modifying Git only changes the desired state. It does not directly execute anything in the cluster. ArgoCD still has to pull the change and reconcile it with the cluster. Because every change goes through Git first, you get a reviewable, auditable record before it reaches production.

And the blast radius shrinks dramatically. A compromised pipeline becomes a much less dangerous event.

Let’s look at how ArgoCD is built:

ArgoCD is not an external service you call into.

It runs as Kubernetes workloads inside the cluster it manages, in the argocd namespace. This is . The agent needs direct access to the Kubernetes API to reconcile state. Running inside the cluster provides the access & keeps cluster credentials inside the cluster.

Here are 5 core components that work together to implement the GitOps reconciliation loop:

API Server is the entry point for everything human-facing in ArgoCD.

It exposes both gRPC & REST APIs consumed by the ArgoCD UI, argocd CLI, and any external tools integrating with ArgoCD. Every user request, whether it comes from the UI, CLI, or an external integration, passes through the API Server.

Also it handles all authentication & authorization.

Before any request reaches the rest of the system, the API Server verifies who is making it and whether they have permission.

The Repo Server does one thing: render Kubernetes manifests from a Git repository.

It clones the repository, reads the source, and generates the manifests ArgoCD will apply to the cluster. It supports plain YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and Jsonnet. Whatever format your configuration lives in, the Repo Server handles the rendering.

It’s deliberately isolated from the Application Controller.

Rendering manifests requires running Helm, Kustomize & Jsonnet. Those processes are often CPU-intensive and occasionally unstable. Keeping the Repo Server separate isolates render failures from the controller’s reconciliation loop.

3. Application Controller

The Application Controller is the heart of ArgoCD…It runs the reconciliation loop.

On every cycle, it gets the desired manifests from the Repo Server and the live cluster state from the Kubernetes API. Then it computes the diff between the two. Based on the application’s sync policy, it either alerts you to the difference or corrects it automatically.

The Application Controller runs as a StatefulSet.

(Scaling and sharding are covered later.)

Redis serves as a cache layer between Application Controller and Kubernetes API.

Without it, every UI load and every reconciliation cycle would need to query the Kubernetes API directly. At scale, this would generate unnecessary load on the Kubernetes API. Redis stores application state and cluster data so repeated reads hit the cache instead of the API.

It is worth being clear about what Redis is and is not in this context.

It is a cache, not a primary data store. ArgoCD does not depend on Redis for correctness. If Redis goes down, ArgoCD degrades gracefully. Performance suffers, but reconciliation continues.

5. Notifications Controller

Notifications Controller watches ArgoCD events & route alerts to external systems.

When an application goes OutOfSync, a sync fails, or a health check degrades, the Notifications Controller sends an alert. It uses the destination you configured, such as Slack, email, PagerDuty, or a webhook. You define triggers and templates, and the controller handles the delivery.

In most production deployments, it gets installed alongside the rest of ArgoCD. It connects ArgoCD’s internal events with the people and systems responsible for responding to them.

Together, these components form ArgoCD's control plane...

Each component has a specific responsibility:

  • API Server handles user requests.

  • Repo Server renders manifests.

  • Application Controller reconciles applications.

  • Redis caches data to reduce repeated API calls.

  • Notifications Controller reports important events.

Together, these components keep the cluster aligned with the desired state in Git.

With the architecture covered, let’s see how these components work together during reconciliation…

When you upgrade, you’ll get:

  • High-level architecture of real-world systems.

  • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

(If this newsletter has helped you become a better software engineer, consider subscribing to support my work.)

How ArgoCD Keeps Your Cluster in Sync

items.title: 11 Networking Concepts Explained in 11 Minutes
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Computer networking is an important part of ALL systems you’ll work on in your engineering career.

While junior developers may get by with writing code, senior engineers are valued for their ability to understand how systems communicate & troubleshoot network problems.

What happens when a network connection fails?

How does data travel between devices & servers?

How do we diagnose slow connections, packet loss & routing problems?

These questions form the foundation of every reliable, high-performing system.

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

  • The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

  • How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

  • Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

(Thanks to Unblocked for partnering on this newsletter.)

Here are all the key concepts that you need to understand computer networking & become a better engineer:

Ethernet is a networking technology that connects devices within a Local Area Network ().

  1. The sender wraps an IP packet inside an Ethernet frame.

  2. Frame contains source & destination Media Access Control () addresses.

  3. The network interface sends the frame over a physical link.

  4. Network switches forward frames toward their destinations using MAC addresses.

  5. The receiver checks the frame’s Frame Check Sequence () to detect transmission errors.

Typical Ethernet speeds include 1 Gbps for desktops, 10 or 25 Gbps for servers, and 100+ Gbps for data center networks.

Imagine delivering packages between offices in the same building.

Each package carries the sender’s & recipient’s room numbers. A mailroom reads the destination and forwards the package to the correct office.

A media access control () address identifies a network card. They help devices communicate within a “local” network.

Every card ships with a 48-bit address, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits. The first half identifies the manufacturer, while the second half identifies the card.

IP addresses move packets between networks, and MAC addresses move frames within one network. A device learns its neighbor’s MAC address by broadcasting a question through the address resolution protocol (), and then caches that answer.

Think of an IP address as a building’s street address and a MAC address as an apartment number.

A switch forwards frames between devices on the “same” network, using their MAC addresses.

A switch learns devices that are reachable through each port by reading the source MAC address of incoming frames. Then it stores these MAC address-to-port mappings in a

  • The switch forwards the frame through the port associated with the destination MAC address.

  • The switch floods the frame through all other ports in the same VLAN until it learns where the destination is located.

A switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network using MAC addresses, while a router forwards IP packets between networks using IP addresses.

Imagine a mailroom in an office building:

The mailroom learns which office belongs to each employee & delivers letters directly to the correct room. If it doesn’t know the destination, it sends copies to every office until it learns where the recipient is.

Wi-Fi is a wireless networking technology that uses radio waves to transmit data between devices.

  • Devices send & receive data using radio signals.

  • Devices use mechanisms such as Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance () to reduce transmission collisions.

  • Wi-Fi operates on 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands.

  • Devices adjust transmission rates based on signal quality & interference.

  • Lost/corrupted frames require retransmission; thus reducing throughput.

The 2.4 GHz band typically provides longer range but has less available capacity & more interference.

The 5 GHz & 6 GHz bands offer wider channels and potentially higher speeds, but their signals have shorter range & weaker penetration through obstacles.

Also devices with poor signal quality transmit at lower data rates and consume more airtime. This reduces the capacity available to other devices sharing the channel.

Imagine a room where people take turns speaking.

Everyone listens before talking to avoid interruptions. If someone far away speaks slowly, others have to wait longer to finish.

A static IP address is a “fixed” IP address assigned to a device or network interface.

You configure it manually or reserve an address through Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol ().

A static IP typically remains the same across device reboots as long as its assignment remains valid. Servers, printers, routers & other devices that need predictable network addresses use static IPs.

DNS records, firewall rules & network configurations reference these stable addresses.

Think of it as a reserved parking space with your name on the sign.

The space stays assigned to you, whether you manage the reservation yourself or someone else manages it.

Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol () automatically assigns IP addresses & other network settings to devices when they join a network.

  1. The device broadcasts a message to find available DHCP servers.

  2. A DHCP server offers an IP address & network configuration.

  3. The device requests the offered address.

  4. Server confirms the assignment & grants an IP address .

(This process is called DORA.)

Plus, DHCP server provides a subnet mask, default gateway, and Domain Name System () servers.

Yet each IP address lease has a lifetime.

Devices typically renew leases before they expire. If a lease expires without renewal, the server reassigns the address to another device.

Imagine checking into a hotel:

The receptionist assigns you a room number for your stay. When you check out, the room becomes available for another guest.

A default gateway is a router that forwards traffic to destinations outside a device’s local network when “no” specific route exists.

  • The device sends traffic directly to another device on the same subnet.

  • The device forwards traffic to its default gateway.

  • Gateway uses its routing table to forward the packet toward its destination.

A laptop with IP address might use as its default gateway.

The gateway typically has an IP address on the same subnet,,, thus allowing the laptop to reach it directly.

An incorrect default gateway prevents a device from reaching “external” networks, even if local communication works.

Think of a building with one main exit.

You move between rooms inside the building without leaving. To reach another building, you must use the main exit.

A static route is a (manually) configured entry in a routing table that tells a router where to forward packets.

You specify a destination IP range & an outgoing network interface.

  • Define a destination network, such as .

  • Point the route to another router, such as .

  • The router uses the route to forward matching traffic toward its destination.

Yet static routes do not automatically learn new network paths.

If a network path fails, the static route still remains configured. Some implementations detect failures & deactivate/replace the route.

Static routes work well for cloud networking configurations.

Imagine a road sign directing drivers toward a specific town.

The sign stays in place even when the road closes, unless someone updates it or a traffic management system redirects drivers.

Open Shortest Path First () is a dynamic routing protocol that lets routers automatically discover & update routes within an Autonomous System ().

  1. Routers exchange Hello packets to discover & maintain neighboring routers.

  2. Routers flood Link-State Advertisements (s) to share network information within an OSPF area.

  3. Routers in the same area maintain a synchronized link-state database.

  4. Each router uses Dijkstra’s Shortest Path First algorithm to calculate the lowest-cost paths.

  5. When a link fails, routers propagate updated information and recalculate affected routes.

OSPF selects paths based on configurable interface costs.

Bandwidth influences these costs, but administrators could adjust them manually.

Plus, OSPF reroutes traffic after network failures. Convergence time depends on failure detection, topology size & router configuration.

Imagine every driver in a city using a shared road map.

When a road closes, the map updates, and each driver calculates a new route based on the available roads.

Internet Control Message Protocol () carries network error messages & diagnostic information. It helps devices identify problems such as unreachable destinations, expired packet lifetimes, and packets too large for a network link.

  • A router or destination host sends an ICMP message when it cannot deliver a packet.

  • A router sends an ICMP message when a packet’s Time to Live () or Hop Limit reaches zero.

  • ICMP reports when a packet exceeds the supported Maximum Transmission Unit ().

  • Tools such as use ICMP to test whether a destination responds.

Yet ICMP messages are NOT guaranteed to arrive…

Firewalls, rate limiting & network conditions could block/drop them.

ICMP helps diagnose network problems but does not directly retransmit lost application data or repair failed connections.

Imagine sending a letter that cannot reach its destination…

The post office returns a notice explaining why delivery failed, such as an invalid address or an unavailable route.

The notice helps you identify the problem, but it does not deliver the original letter.

Ping is a network diagnostic tool that tests whether a destination host responds & measures round-trip time (). It uses ICMP Echo Request & Echo Reply messages.

  1. Ping sends an ICMP Echo Request to the destination.

  2. If the destination responds, it sends an ICMP Echo Reply.

  3. Ping calculates time between sending request & receiving reply.

  4. Ping reports round-trip times & percentage of requests without replies.

Repeated tests help identify latency spikes, intermittent connectivity & potential packet loss.

Imagine knocking on a door & timing how long someone takes to answer.

A quick response suggests someone is available. A delayed response takes longer, while silence only means nobody answered.

Now you understand the basic networking concepts that help devices communicate, it’s time to explore how they work in real systems.

Look at the apps & networks you use every day and think about what happens behind the scenes.

What happens when a network link fails?

How does your laptop connect to the internet?

How do routers find the right path for packets?

How do engineers diagnose slow or failed connections?

After understanding these concepts, start applying them in your own work.

Use tools like , , and to explore network behavior. Experiment with routing configurations and troubleshoot connectivity problems.

Remember, every experienced engineer started with the fundamentals. The more you practice, the easier it becomes to understand and troubleshoot complex networks.

items.title: The 80/20 of AI Concepts
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Long-running agents need endurance.

They must endure waiting for users and weather tool failures. They must take each new jump in model intelligence in stride.

Inngest makes long-running agents durable, observable and improvable over time.

(Thanks to Inngest for partnering on this newsletter.)

The 80/20 rule states that 80% of results come from 20% of actions.

It is the ONE rule you must obey & this is the most important rule when it comes to learning something new.

Imagine you want to fill a bottle with pebbles, sand & water.

If you pour in the sand & water first, you’ll struggle to fit the big pebbles.

But if you start with the pebbles, the sand fills the gaps between them, and the water fills the remaining space.

i.e., do the 20% that makes the real difference (80%) first.

And this is why I’m writing these letters on AI engineering concepts for you.

I want you to win in the AI era by understanding the “fundamental” AI concepts.

Inside this newsletter, you’ll find:

  1. Large Language Model Serving & Inference Engines,

  2. Synthetic Data & Self-Instruction,

  3. Direct Preference Optimization,

  4. Gradient Descent & Optimization,

  • What it means & how it works,

  • A real-world analogy where useful,

  • A common mistake to avoid,

Mixture-of-Experts () is a model design that uses a router to direct information to neural network components called . Common sparse designs activate only some experts for each token.

Let’s look inside a model as it processes a question:

Imagine one layer contains eight experts. A router selects two experts to process a token’s numerical representation. Then the layer combines their results & passes the information onward.

The next token could use a different pair of experts.

The router learns how to assign work during training. Each expert performs part of the model’s calculations, while other components also contribute to the response.

(These experts work within the same model.)

Think of a workshop with several workers & a coordinator.

The coordinator assigns each task to a few workers. Those workers contribute their results, and the work continues through the workshop.

Not every worker needs to handle every piece.

Assuming each expert has a fixed subject - mathematics, coding, or history.

The word “expert” describes a neural network component. Training shapes its behavior & router’s choices, but those choices don’t necessarily follow recognizable subject categories.

Sparse MoE allows a model to have more parameters using all its experts for every token. Only selected experts perform calculations, thus reducing computation while giving the model more capacity to learn patterns.

Yet all expert weights still need to be stored in memory/storage.

So using fewer experts per token reduces computation, but doesn’t reduce the model’s memory requirements.

36. LLM Serving and Inference Engines

LLM serving makes a trained model available to receive requests & return responses. An inference engine is the software that runs the model’s calculations.

You submit through a chatbot:

  1. The serving system accepts your request & passes it to the software that runs the model.

  2. Inference engine uses the model’s weights & your input to generate tokens.

  3. The serving system sends those tokens back to your screen.

Your answer arrives through several coordinated steps.

Now imagine hundreds of users submitting questions at once...

The system schedules work within the available memory & computing capacity. Some requests need longer responses than others. Requests that exceed available capacity must wait or get rejected.

The model needs software around it to serve real users.

Think of a restaurant’s kitchen & service team:

The kitchen prepares the meals… The wider restaurant operation accepts orders, coordinates workload, and delivers food to customers.

Preparing a meal is one part of serving a restaurant full of people.

Testing one request & assuming the system is ready for traffic.

A setup that responds quickly to one user could slow down when many requests arrive at once. Test realistic request volumes & response lengths, then check waiting times, failures & memory use.

LLM serving helps applications handle requests from many users.

While inference engines run the model’s calculations to generate responses. Together, they affect response time, hardware efficiency, and how reliably an application serves users.

Choosing a suitable engine & testing the complete serving system helps turn a trained model into a dependable service.

37. Synthetic Data and Self-Instruction

Synthetic data is “artificially created” data used for purposes such as training/testing. Self-instruction uses a language model to generate tasks & corresponding responses for further training.

Imagine you need more training examples for a model that classifies “customer support” messages.

You ask a language model to generate fictional messages about billing & technical problems.

With , the model also creates instructions & expected answers for those messages.

Each example contains a task & its correct label:

  • Instruction: Classify this customer message.

  • Message: “My card got charged twice.”

  • Expected answer: Billing.

The system then checks generated examples & removes incorrect, repetitive, and/or unsuitable ones.

The remaining examples could be used to the model…

Also generating examples alone doesn’t change the model’s weights… A separate training step uses those examples to update the weights, thus helping the model learn to classify similar messages.

Think of preparing practice questions with an answer key:

You create exercises to cover different situations. Before anyone studies from them, you check whether the questions make sense & if the answers are correct.

Faulty practice material teaches faulty lessons.

Treating a large generated dataset as a high-quality dataset.

Generated examples could contain wrong answers, repeated patterns, or unrealistic situations. Check their accuracy & variety, then evaluate the trained model on separate examples that reflect real use.

  • Synthetic data helps expand training material when suitable examples are scarce.

  • Self-instruction provides one way to create examples for instruction-based tasks.

The value comes from useful, checked examples rather than volume alone.

LLM-as-a-Judge uses a language model to evaluate another model’s responses against predefined criteria, such as factual accuracy, relevance, or completeness, and assigns scores/rankings based on those criteria.

Ask an assistant to shorten a customer’s complaint.

The customer wrote, “My order arrived three days late, and the box was damaged.” But the assistant produces “The order arrived late.” You give a judge model both versions & ask it to check whether the summary includes both problems.

The judge could flag the missing detail:

Your instructions define what the judge checks. It could score one response, explain a problem, or compare two answers & select the better one.

Clear criteria give the review a specific purpose.

Think of a teacher checking a student’s work:

The teacher compares the answer to the assignment requirements. A judge model performs a similar review using the instructions and reference material you supply.

Treating the judge’s score as proof of correctness.

A judge could overlook an error or favor a longer answer without good reason. Compare some of its reviews with careful human assessments. When comparing 2 answers, swap their order to check whether its preference changes.

Reading every response by hand takes time.

LLM judges help teams review large collections of answers & identify responses that need closer inspection.

Their usefulness depends on how reliably their assessments match qualities you need.

39. Direct Preference Optimization

Direct Preference Optimization () “trains” a language model to favor preferred responses over less preferred alternatives using pairs of answers to the same request.

Imagine you want an assistant to reply politely to customers.

For one response says, Another says, “I’m sorry about the delay. Please send your order number.” A reviewer marks the second response as the better choice.

The pair then becomes a training example.

DPO uses many such pairs to adjust the model’s weights toward preferred responses during training. It uses recorded choices directly, without first training a separate reward model to score answers.

Choosing a response records feedback; the training step changes the model.

Think of helping someone write customer replies:

You show two drafts & point out which one better follows the company’s standards. Repeated practice guides how the person writes future replies.

DPO guides a model through similar comparisons.

Choosing preferred answers based only on how pleasant they sound.

A polite reply could promise a refund the customer doesn’t qualify for. Review accuracy & company policy alongside tone, so the training examples reward useful behavior.

DPO provides a simpler way to train from preferences than approaches which require a separate reward model and reinforcement learning.

The quality of those preferences shapes the behavior the model learns.

40. Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation a student model to learn from a teacher model’s outputs. A common goal is to preserve useful abilities in a smaller model.

Imagine a large model recognizes cats & dogs well, but your application needs something smaller.

You show photos to the teacher model & collect its predictions. The student processes the same photos, and the training algorithm compares its predictions to the teacher’s. Then it adjusts student’s weights to bring their predictions closer together.

The teacher’s outputs guide the student’s training.

Some methods also use the teacher’s confidence across possible answers. This gives the student more information than a single label such as “cat.” The student learns through its own weight adjustments.

After training, the student handles new photos independently.

Think of a teacher helping a student practice.

The teacher demonstrates answers, and the student learns from those examples. The student attempts new questions later without the teacher beside them.

Practice doesn’t guarantee the student matches the teacher on every question.

Assuming the student inherits every ability the teacher has.

A student trained on cat & dog photos hasn’t necessarily learned to recognize other animals. It could also repeat the teacher’s errors. Test it on separate examples which reflect the job you need it to perform.

Distillation helps teams develop models which need less memory and computation for a chosen task. A smaller student could serve requests faster or run on more limited hardware.

Check whether those savings preserve the quality your application needs.

41. Temperature and Sampling

Sampling is how an AI model chooses the next token during inference. Tokens the model considers likely have a higher chance of being chosen.

Temperature controls how predictable that choice is by adjusting the probabilities to make likely options more dominant or give less likely options more chance.

Ask an assistant to suggest a name for your bakery:

The model builds each suggestion one token at a time. At each step, it assigns probabilities to possible next tokens. Sampling chooses among those options according to their chances.

Different choices lead to different names.

Lower temperature favors the leading options more strongly, usually producing less variation across attempts. Higher temperature gives less likely options more chance, usually producing more varied suggestions.

Yet some results could be unusual/awkward… More variation doesn’t guarantee a better name.

These settings affect token selection changing the model’s weights.

Think of drawing a slip from a bowl.

Several slips carry the same word, while others carry different words. A word with more slips has a higher chance of being selected.

Temperature changes the balance of slips; sampling makes the draw.

Treating temperature as a quality control.

A higher setting doesn’t guarantee originality, and a lower setting doesn’t guarantee accuracy. Review results for readability & relevance, and check factual answers against reliable sources.

Different tasks need different amounts of variation…

Name suggestions benefit from a range of options, while extracting details from a receipt benefits from consistent results.

Test the settings against the task rather than using one value for everything.

items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
“Hi Neo, do I really need to understand all these AI concepts? RLHF, vector search, quantization, diffusion models, MCP, hybrid retrieval... It feels like every time I learn one concept, five more appear. Lol”

You don’t need to master every AI concept to start building AI apps.

At least, not all at once.

But understanding how these concepts work makes a BIG difference.

Most teams choose a coding agent by its model. AgentField tested the other half: ten coding harnesses on one open model, run on the same 113 real GitHub issues from the DeepSWE benchmark. Results ran from 3 solved issues to 62. The system around the model decides as much as the model does.

, a new open-source coding harness by AgentField AI, finished #1 of the ten (method and data are public on GitHub):

  • 2x OpenCode’s solves and nearly 4x Claude Code’s, on the same model

  • 4.8x less per solved issue than OpenCode, 3.4x less than Claude Code

  • Built for open models like DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Kimi, and it works with closed models too

  • One small Go binary, open source

(Thanks to AgentField for partnering on this newsletter.)

This is part 2 of a four-part newsletter series:

  1. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback,

  2. Vector Search and Approximate Nearest Neighbors,

  3. Hallucination, Factuality and Grounding,

  4. Context Windows and Long-Context Modeling,

  5. Structured Outputs and Constrained Decoding,

  6. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning,

  7. Autoregressive Generation and Next-Token Prediction,

  8. Self-Supervised Learning,

  9. Chunking and Document Segmentation.

( …and much more in Parts 3 & 4!)

  • What it means & how it works,

  • A real-world analogy where useful,

  • A common mistake to avoid,

18. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback () uses human feedback to guide further model training toward preferred responses.

Give reviewers two answers to the same question.

The reviewers compare qualities such as usefulness & how well each answer follows instructions. Those comparisons train a reward model to score responses. The language model then receives further training to produce responses with higher scores.

Human preferences help shape what the training process rewards.

This improves behavior according to the chosen criteria, but still needs careful evaluation.

Think of a coach reviewing practice performances:

Feedback guides the next attempt. The improvement depends partly on whether the coach rewards the qualities the task actually requires.

Confusing a preferred answer with a “verified” answer.

Reviewers could favor a polished response containing a subtle factual error. Check accuracy separately from tone & helpfulness.

RLHF helps shape a broadly trained model into a more useful assistant. The feedback criteria influence which behaviors the model learns to favor.

Pretraining is an initial training stage in which a model learns broad patterns from a large dataset before more specialized training.

Before a model follows your request, it needs a foundation.

For a typical generative language model, pretraining repeatedly tests predictions of the next token. Prediction errors guide adjustments to the model’s weights. Across many examples, these adjustments help the model learn patterns in the text.

The text itself supplies the next-token answers.

Other models use different tasks, such as predicting missing pieces of an input.

Think of a broad education before a specialized course:

The foundation covers many subjects & patterns. Later instruction directs those abilities toward a particular role.

Assuming pretraining produces a ready-to-use assistant.

A model trained to predict text doesn’t automatically respond in the style users expect. Further training & application design help shape how it handles requests.

Pretraining provides capabilities reused across many tasks.

The data influences what the model learns well and where its knowledge has gaps.

20. Vector Search and Approximate Nearest Neighbors

Vector search finds items with similar numerical representations. Approximate Nearest Neighbors () methods speed up search while accepting the possibility of some closest matches.

Imagine searching millions of support documents:

The system converts your question into an embedding & compares it with document embeddings with . An exact finds the closest matches under a chosen comparison rule. An uses an index, an organized search structure, to reduce the work.

The shortcut helps results arrive faster.

How much accuracy it sacrifices depends on the method & its settings…

Think of a librarian directing you to likely shelves…

You search a smaller area instead of checking every book. The shortcut saves time, but you could miss a useful book elsewhere.

Choosing the fastest setup without checking its results.

A quick search is unhelpful if it repeatedly misses the relevant document. Compare retrieval quality, response time & memory use.

  • Vector Search: Best for datasets requiring the true nearest matches.

  • Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Best for datasets where search speed & scalability matter more than finding the exact nearest match.

In-context learning is a model’s ability to use instructions/examples in its current context without updating its weights.

Show the model a few examples before asking it to label a new message:

“My card was charged twice” → Billing

“The page crashes when I sign in” → Technical

The examples demonstrate the categories & response format. The model then uses the pattern to label the next message. No separate training run occurs!

The examples the response through the context.

(Remove them from a later request, and you shouldn’t assume the model still has access to them.)

Think of filling out a form after examining a completed sample:

The sample shows how the fields work. You apply the pattern immediately without taking a new course.

Providing examples that cover only obvious cases.

If every billing example contains “invoice,” the model could rely too heavily on a specific word. Include varied wording & difficult cases, then test on separate examples.

In-context learning lets you demonstrate a task quickly. It helps you test formats/categories before investing in fine-tuning.

22. Hallucination, Factuality, and Grounded Answers

A hallucination is generated content presented as “true” despite being false/unsupported. Factuality concerns correctness; grounding connects an answer to evidence.

An assistant gives you a confident answer & 3 citations.

One source doesn’t exist. Another exists without supporting the claim. The answer looks well researched, but its appearance tells you little about its accuracy.

The evidence needs inspection too…

A answer uses supplied or retrieved material. It could still repeat an error from an outdated source, so the material's quality matters.

Think of a report with footnotes.

The footnotes help you trace the claims. You still need to check whether the sources exist & support what the report says.

Treating a citation as a completed fact-check.

Check the source & compare its content with the answer. Give the system a way to report insufficient evidence instead of filling gaps with guesses.

These distinctions help you find the source of an error. The application could need better documents, better retrieval, and/or stricter checks on the final answer.

Quantization stores model values using fewer bits, thus reducing memory needs while preserving less numerical details.

A model is too large for your machine's memory.

Its weights are numbers, and storing those numbers takes space. Quantization converts selected values into numerical representations. The model needs less memory, though the conversion introduces .

You trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint.

The effect on output quality depends on the model & the quantization method.

Think of recording measurements to the nearest centimeter instead of millimeters.

You preserve less detail. Whether the difference matters depends on what you need the measurements for.

Assuming a smaller model representation always runs faster with identical results.

Speed depends on the hardware & software used to run it. Test both quality and response time before choosing a quantized version.

Quantization helps larger models fit within smaller memory budgets. It creates more deployment options when the quality tradeoff is acceptable.

24. Context Windows and Long-Context Models

A context window is the amount of information a model handles within a single context (measured in tokens). Long-context models support larger amounts of material.

Upload a long manual & ask about a detail halfway through it.

Your instructions, conversation history, document text, and tool results all take up space. In typical text-generation systems, the response also needs room within the overall limit. The application decides what to include & how much space to reserve for the answer.

A larger window holds more material.

Yet it doesn’t guarantee the model uses every detail correctly.

Think of a desk covered with reference pages.

A larger desk holds more pages. It doesn’t guarantee you notice every detail or connect the right passages.

Assuming a document that fits is a document the model uses reliably.

Test questions whose answers appear in different parts of the document. Remove irrelevant material or retrieve targeted passages when full-document answers become unreliable.

Context limits affect document analysis, code review & long conversations. Plus the amount of material processed influences cost & response time.

25. Structured Outputs and Constrained Decoding

Structured outputs follow a specified format. Constrained decoding restricts what model generates, so the output follows supported format rules.

Your application needs 3 fields from a support ticket.

A paragraph is inconvenient for code to process. A schema, or set of format rules, defines the field names, value types, and permitted choices. limits the model’s next-token options to keep the response within those rules.

This makes the result easier for software to process.

For example, a could follow a JSON schema like this

{
 “category”: “billing”,
 “priority”: “high”,
 “order_id”: null
}

Think of a form with fixed fields & dropdown menus.

The form controls where information goes & which options are allowed. It doesn’t establish whether the selected option is correct.

Confusing correct format with correct .

A response could follow every format rule and still misclassify a ticket. Check the values and handle refusals or incomplete responses separately.

Structured outputs reduce work needed to turn model responses into usable application data. They solve a formatting problem, while factual checks remain necessary.

26. Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol () is an open standard for connecting AI apps to external tools & information sources.

Your assistant needs access to a document store & a ticket system.

An MCP server exposes capabilities, such as a document search or ticket lookup. The AI application connects through an MCP client, which discovers those capabilities and exchanges requests & results. The shared protocol gives both sides a common way to communicate.

The connection follows a standard format.

(The application & connected services still need to enforce access permissions.)

Think of a connector between devices:

A shared connector reduces custom wiring. Each device still offers different capabilities & plugging it in doesn’t grant permission to use everything.

Treating an MCP server as automatically trusted.

A server could expose sensitive data or powerful actions. Review its capabilities, limit permissions & decide which actions need approval.

MCP reduces custom integration work across compatible AI applications.

A server’s capabilities become reusable without designing a different communication interface for every application.

27. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and LoRA

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning () adapts a model by training only a small portion of its parameters or added parameters. Low-Rank Adaptation () is one method that learns compact additions to selected model weights.

You want a model to follow your support team’s response style.

Full fine-tuning updates all of the model’s weights. LoRA keeps the original weights fixed and trains smaller groups of numbers that represent changes to selected layers. These learned additions influence the model’s output.

The additions are then saved as an adapter.

The adapter works alongside the base model, or its changes are merged into compatible weights.

Think of a company handbook with a short for each department:

The main handbook stays the same. Each supplement adapts to a specific role. A LoRA adapter serves a similar purpose through learned numerical changes.

Assuming a small adapter works with any model.

Its changes depend on the base model & layers used during training. Keep the matching model version and configuration, then test the combined result on separate examples.

PEFT reduces the resources needed to train and store specialized adaptations.

The base model still needs memory and computation, but maintaining several task-specific versions becomes more practical.

I spent a few hours putting together this list of foundational networking concepts, so you don’t have to.

Curious to know how many are new to you:

    • What it is & how it works in simple words,

    The network stack divides communication into layers. Each layer handles a specific task & passes data to the next layer.

    Two models explain how these layers work:

    • The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model has 7 layers. It helps you understand and troubleshoot network communication.

    • The Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) model has four layers: Application, Transport, Internet, and Link. It reflects how modern internet protocols work.

    Think about opening a website:

    Your browser sends an HTTP request. The transport layer manages communication between applications, the internet layer routes packets toward their destination, and the link layer delivers data across the local network.

    Each layer handles its own responsibility.

    So your app does not have to manage packet routing or physical transmission.

    A letter passing through the postal system:

    You write the words. An envelope carries the address; a sorting office picks the route; and a truck moves the physical mail. Each stage trusts the next to do its job.

    Imagine your application suddenly loses its database connection…

    The problem could occur in several places:

    • DNS fails to resolve the database hostname.

    • A firewall blocks the database’s TCP port.

    • Transport/Application boundary: A TLS handshake fails.

    • A routing issue prevents packets from reaching the database.

    Understanding the network stack helps you identify where communication fails & narrow down the root cause.

    Reach for when you suspect the transport, and when you suspect the application. Pair it with encapsulation, which shows what each layer adds to your data.

    Encapsulation is the process of wrapping data with protocol headers as it moves down the network stack.

    When you send an HTTP request, each layer adds information needed to deliver data:

    1. Creates the HTTP request containing the payload.

    2. Adds a TCP header with source & destination ports, sequence numbers, and control information.

    3. Adds an IP header with source & destination IP addresses.

    4. Wraps the IP packet in an Ethernet frame with a header & trailer.

    The receiving machine reverses this process; it’s called .

    Each layer processes its protocol information & passes remaining data to layer above.

    A gift in a box, inside a padded parcel, inside a shipping crate.

    Each wrapper carries the label its own handler needs, and nobody opens more than one layer.

    Every header adds overhead to network communication.

    Sending a 10-byte payload over TCP/IPv4 and Ethernet requires:

    • Ethernet header and trailer: 18 bytes

    • Application payload: 10 bytes

    That’s 58 bytes of protocol overhead for just 10 bytes of payload, excluding Ethernet padding and other link-level overhead.

    Small messages consume significantly more bandwidth than their payload size suggests.

    Read frames with and set path sizes in your virtual private network config. Read it alongside ports and sockets, which explain the transport header fields.

    An Internet Protocol () address identifies a network interface & helps routers deliver packets to the correct destination.

    There are two main versions:

    • Uses 32-bit addresses, such as . It supports 4.3 billion unique addresses.

    • Uses 128-bit addresses, such as . It provides a vastly larger address space.

    IPv4 addresses became as the Internet grew…

    To conserve public addresses, networks adopted Network Address Translation (). This allows many devices to share one public IPv4 address.

    IPv6 addresses this limitation by providing enough addresses for an enormous number of devices & networks.

    Plus, many networks support both IPv4 & IPv6, an approach called .

    • Your laptop could have both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address.

    • A website could publish both IPv4 () and IPv6 () DNS records.

    • Your device selects a reachable address & connects using corresponding protocol.

    IPv6 adoption varies across networks…

    Some mobile carriers and cloud providers support it extensively, while many corporate networks still rely on IPv4.

    Think of IPv4 as a city running out of house addresses.

    IPv6 expands the address space so dramatically that there is room for an enormous number of new buildings.

    When designing a cloud network, you need to choose which IP versions to support.

    • Configure IPv4-only, dual-stack, or IPv6-only subnets according to your requirements.

    • Configure IPv4, IPv6, or dual-stack networking based on your cluster and Container Network Interface (CNI) support.

    Also you need to understand .

    It divides an IP address range into smaller networks for routing & address management.

was supposed to make the web faster.

It introduced multiplexing, header compression & better connection reuse.

But one lost TCP packet could still delay every stream on the connection.

was built to solve this problem.

In this newsletter, we’ll break down 12 essential concepts behind & :

  1. HPACK header compression,

  2. Server push & early hints,

  3. TCP head-of-line blocking,

  4. Independent streams & loss recovery,

  5. Connection IDs & connection migration,

  6. Alt-Svc & HTTPS DNS records.

  • What it is & how it works in simple words,

Multiplexing sends many requests & responses at the same time over ONE connection by interleaving their frames.

Request one waits on a slow database while other requests return & render. The server replies in whatever order the data becomes ready.

The result shows up plainly in connection counts:

A desktop page opens connections on than on . The gap roughly doubles on lighter pages, where one connection does the work of two.

One conversation channel where each sentence carries the speaker’s name.

Three people talk at once, and nobody loses the thread.

Multiplexing changes how you bundle because many tiny files beat a large one for cache reuse.

Confirm which protocol your assets use with the devtools protocol column and measure the bundling change in WebPageTest. Yet TCP head-of-line blocking marks the limit multiplexing could never remove.

13. HPACK Header Compression

HPACK is the header compression format for .

It’s built from a static table, a dynamic table & Huffman coding.

Headers repeat almost perfectly. Your string, headers, and go out identically on every request, and on an API-heavy page they outweigh the payload.

A fixed table of common header names covers the obvious cases, so a method line becomes a single byte. Headers you have already sent go into a dynamic table shared by both ends.

The second request references those entries by number rather than repeating them, and the saving compounds across every request on the connection.

Shorthand between two colleagues who talk daily.

Once you both agree a short name means one specific document, you stop saying the full title.

Header weight decides real latency on pages carrying large authentication tokens.

Inspect encoded header sizes in Wireshark and compare them against the devtools network panel. QPACK rebuilds this idea for out-of-order delivery.

Flow control limits how much data a sender may have outstanding, applied per stream & across the whole connection.

The receiver sets a flow-control window. This limits how much DATA the sender can transmit before receiving additional flow-control credit. A frame grants more room as the receiver consumes data, and the default initial window is 65,535 bytes.

This mechanism protects slow consumers:

A browser decoding a large image should slow the pipe rather than buffer forever, and a proxy feeding a slow client behaves the same way.

Also it stops one greedy stream from monopolizing a connection everything else depends on.

A coworker saying, “Send me five files at a time, and I will ask for more.”

They control the pace, so nothing piles up on their desk.

Large uploads, gRPC streams, and video segments all hit this ceiling before they hit bandwidth.

Watch window updates with and confirm socket-level throughput with . Independent streams show how QUIC applies the same idea per stream.

15. Stream Prioritization

Stream prioritization lets a client tell the server which responses matter most, so the server can send that data first.

A browser needs CSS to render a webpage. Giving CSS higher priority than a large image helps the page become usable quicker, even if the total amount of data stays the same.

used a complex system of stream dependencies & weights to decide which data to send first. But browsers & servers struggled to implement it consistently!

Then a simpler priority scheme got introduced... It uses 2 signals:

  • Indicates how important a response is. Zero is the highest priority & seven is the lowest.

  • Indicates whether a response can be delivered progressively, thus allowing the server to interleave its data with other responses.

Also browsers provide the Fetch Priority API.

This lets developers influence the priority of resources using attributes such as .

The browser uses these hints when scheduling requests and assigning HTTP priorities, although the Fetch Priority API does not directly expose HTTP’s urgency values.

Adoption of the Fetch Priority API grew rapidly after Chrome introduced support.

Everyone in the waiting room gets seen & order reflects who needs help soonest.

One attribute on your largest visible image moves a headline performance metric.

Set fetchpriority in your markup and verify the assigned value in the Chrome devtools priority column. Early hints reach the same goal from the server side.

16. Server Push and Early Hints

Server Push lets a server send resources to a browser before browser requests them.

It was one of ’s most promising features.

Servers pushed files already stored in the browser’s cache, thus wasting bandwidth. Also performance improvements were inconsistent, so adoption remained low.

(Chrome eventually disabled Server Push by default, and Firefox removed support.)

Early Hints emerged as a simpler alternative:

Instead of sending the resource itself, the server sends an HTTP response containing headers while preparing the final response.

The browser then uses these hints to:

  • Establish connections to other servers before they’re needed.

  • Start downloading crucial resources, such as CSS files, before the final HTML arrives.

This helps the browser start useful work earlier & potentially render the page faster.

Yet adoption remains limited… Only 2.9% of desktop pages used Early Hints, with Shopify accounting for roughly 90% of those deployments.

Push is a waiter setting down a dish you never ordered & may already have.

Early hints is a waiter handing you the menu while the kitchen warms up.

Dead push configuration survives in production long after browsers stopped honoring it.

Enable early hints at Cloudflare/Fastly and prove the gain with real user monitoring rather than a lab score. Chunked transfer encoding fills the same dead time once the response finally starts.

17. TCP Head-of-Line Blocking

TCP delivers data to applications in a strict order.

If a TCP packet gets lost, later data must wait until the missing packet gets retransmitted. Yet this creates a problem for …

multiplexes multiple streams over one TCP connection. And TCP sees only a single ordered sequence of bytes, with no knowledge of individual streams. So one lost TCP packet delays data delivery across multiple streams, even when their data has already arrived.

This is called TCP head-of-line () blocking.

TCP uses acknowledgments & retransmissions to provide reliable, ordered delivery.

But this ordering can delay otherwise available data… On lossy networks, using one TCP connection sometimes performs worse than using six parallel connections.

Each TCP connection handles packet loss independently, so a lost packet on one connection does not directly block the others.

One conveyor belt at a sorting depot.

Drop a box & everything behind it stops moving, even if those parcels have nothing to do with each other.

This single property is the entire reason exists.
