items.title: HTTP1 vs HTTP2 vs HTTP3
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Why does a site take several seconds to load, even if server responds in milliseconds?

Before a single page appears, the browser must establish connections, send requests, and receive responses…

Understanding underlying mechanisms changed how I think about HTTP & web performance.

In this newsletter, I’ll break down must-know HTTP concepts. Some of these are foundational & some are quite advanced.

All of them are useful to engineers building production-ready systems:

  1. HTTP head-of-line blocking,

  2. Chunked transfer encoding,

  3. Caching & conditional requests,

  4. Parallel connections & domain sharding,

  5. The binary framing layer,

  6. Streams, messages & frames.

(…and much more in Part 2!)

  • What it is & how it works in simple words,

1. Request-Response Cycle

Every HTTP exchange is one request and one response.

The client sends a method, a path, and a set of headers. The server replies with a status code, its own headers, and usually a body. In , the message format is text-based, so you could type a request by hand into a terminal and read the reply with your own eyes.

The earliest version of the protocol supported a single method and returned a single file type. The next version added headers, status codes, POST, and HEAD.

Also, it opened a fresh connection for every exchange and threw it away afterward. (This decision shaped the next 20+ years of workarounds.)

You write one item, mail it, and wait for one parcel.

To order a second item, you write a second postcard.

Debugging an unexpected status code starts with reading the raw exchange, not your application logs.

Send requests by hand with and inspect real traffic in the Chrome DevTools Network tab. The binary framing layer picks up from here, keeping these semantics and changing the bytes.

2. TCP Three-Way Handshake

Transmission Control Protocol () opens a connection with 3 messages before either side sends data.

  1. Client sends a synchronize packet.

  2. Server replies with an acknowledgment plus its own sequence number.

  3. Client acknowledges the number & connection opens.

Three messages cost one full round trip…

i.e., on a link with 100ms of latency, you burn 100ms before the first byte of your request leaves the machine.

Encryption adds more on top…

A Transport Layer Security () 1.2 handshake costs two extra round trips, and TLS 1.3 cut that to one.

You dial, they say hello, and you say hello back. And only on the fourth breath does anyone say something useful.

Connection setup shows up in your p99 long before your handler code does.

Measure it with and watch it across a full page load in WebPageTest. Persistent connections spread that cost across many requests.

3. Persistent Connections

A persistent connection stays open after a response, so the next request reuses it.

made this the default behavior. The connection lives until either side sends a close header or a timeout fires, so one handshake now covers dozens of requests.

The saving compounds on real pages.

A page with 40 assets used to pay 40 handshakes; on a single persistent connection, it pays one.

Keeping the phone line open between questions instead of hanging up and redialing every time you think of something new.

Connection churn on a busy proxy exhausts temporary ports well before it exhausts bandwidth.

Tune in nginx and in Node.js, then check both against your load balancer. TCP slow start explains why a reused connection also runs faster.

Pipelining lets a client send several requests back-to-back on one connection without waiting for each response.

The browser asks for two images at once rather than asking, waiting, then asking again. On paper, it removes a full round trip per request while using nothing more than the connection you already have.

Responses must return in the exact order the requests went out, so a slow first response stalls everything behind it. Buggy proxies mangled pipelined traffic on top of that.

(NOTE: Because of these problems, major browsers disabled pipelining, and it never gained widespread adoption.)

Ordering all three courses at once:

The kitchen still serves them in the order you named them, so a slow starter holds up your main.

You will find pipelining disabled in and every browser, and now you know why.

Confirm the behavior with and watch real request ordering in Wireshark. Multiplexing solves the same problem without the ordering rule.

5. HTTP Head-of-Line Blocking

Head-of-line blocking occurs when first item in a queue delays every item behind it.

One connection processes one exchange at a time:

A slow database query on request one could keep four other requests waiting, and the network sits idle while the queue holds.

This is the ceiling could never lift… Persistent connections removed the handshake cost and left the queue completely intact.

Every workaround built on top of it, from parallel connections to asset bundling, exists to hide this single property.

A single supermarket checkout:

The shopper at the front needs a price check, and the four people behind them stand still.

Stair-stepped requests with visible gaps in a waterfall chart point straight at this.

Read the waterfall in WebPageTest and count concurrent requests in the Chrome DevTools Network panel. Parallel connections show the workaround the browsers actually picked.

6. Chunked Transfer Encoding

Chunked transfer encoding lets a server send a response in pieces without knowing the total size in advance.

The server marks the response as chunked and writes each piece with its size in hexadecimal on the line above. A “zero-length” chunk marks the end.

The browser could start rendering before the full response arrives.

In , chunked transfer encoding supports streaming generated HTML, server-sent events, and token-by-token model responses.

and use DATA frames instead.

A publisher shipping a book one chapter at a time.

You start reading chapter one while the author is still writing chapter four.

Streaming responses depend on the HTTP version’s framing mechanism, and accidental buffering often stops streaming.

Check in nginx and in Express before you blame your application code. Early hints apply the same idea to the wait before a response starts.

7. Caching and Conditional Requests

Caching stores a copy of a response so a later request skips the network entirely.

sets the rules:

A directive says how long a copy stays fresh; forces a check on every use, and promises the file never changes under its URL.

Conditional requests handle the check cheaply:

The client sends its stored entity tag in an header, and a server holding the same version answers without a body.

A cache hit costs zero bytes on the wire and zero milliseconds of server time, thus making it the cheapest performance work available to you.

Asking a librarian whether the report changed since your last visit.

If nothing changed, you read the copy already on your desk.

Static assets & API responses need opposite caching policies, and mixing them up costs freshness or bandwidth.

Set the rules at the edge in Cloudflare/Varnish and read the real cache hit ratio there rather than trusting your config. Conditional requests lose their value once you version filenames properly.

8. Parallel Connections and Domain Sharding

Browsers open several TCP connections (typically 6) to the same origin at once.

Six lanes beat one lane, so head-of-line blocking hurts less. Sites wanting more than six invented extra hostnames, serving images from one subdomain & scripts from another. That bought another six per name.

This technique is called … It shaped front-end architecture.

But it became obsolete the moment multiplexing arrived… yet survives in production long after the sites that used it moved on…

Opening more checkout lanes.

When six lanes fill up, you rent the shop next door and open six more.

Removing dead shards is one of the easier wins available on an older codebase.

Measure the before and after in WebPageTest and let Lighthouse flag the redundant origins. TCP slow start explains why those extra connections start slow.

Slow start is a congestion control algorithm where a new connection begins with a small send window & then grows it each round trip.

TCP has no idea how much bandwidth sits between you and your user. Guessing high floods the path and drops packets, so it guesses low and probes upward instead.

The window typically starts at 10 packets, roughly 14 kilobytes, and doubles on every successful round trip. Packet loss halves it and switches the sender to a slower climb.

Without this algorithm, every new connection would flood the path and collapse throughput for everyone sharing it.

You accelerate in stages instead of flooring it blind into traffic you cannot see yet.

The first 14 kilobytes of your HTML carry more weight than the next 500.

Put critical CSS & your hero image reference inside that window and let Lighthouse confirm the render path. Persistent connections keep the window you already earned.

Binary framing layer encodes HTTP messages as binary frames instead of plain text lines.

Each frame carries a length, type, set of flags, and a stream identifier in a fixed nine-byte header. The methods, headers, and status codes stay exactly as they were.

You still send … You still read . The bytes on the wire look completely different, and frames parse faster and pack tighter than text ever did.

The stream identifier is the important part, and the next concept explains why.

Shipping containers replacing loose cargo.

The goods are identical, and the uniform box is what lets a crane stack, sort, and interleave them at speed.

Reading traffic needs different tools than reading traffic.

Dump frames with nghttp and decode full sessions in Wireshark with a TLS key log. Streams & frames explain what the identifier inside each frame does.

11. Streams, Messages, and Frames

A connection carries many streams; each stream carries one request-response pair, and each message splits into frames tagged with a stream identifier.

i.e., three levels, one job.

The identifier lets frames from different requests share the wire and still reassemble correctly at the far end.

Numbering follows a simple rule:

Client-initiated streams take odd numbers, server-initiated streams take even ones, and identifiers always increase.

A stream costs only a few bytes per frame to label; this is what makes concurrency on a single connection practical.

One highway with many lanes.

Every car carries a destination label, so they travel together and still arrive at different lanes.

Default stream limits rarely match the concurrency your service actually sees.

Set http2_max_concurrent_streams in nginx and the matching limit in Envoy against your real p99. Flow control decides how much data those streams may send.

made the web faster, but it left one major problem unsolved: responses still had to arrive in order on each connection.

addressed this with multiplexing… But TCP’s head-of-line blocking remained.

In Part 2, we’ll explore how & tackled these bottlenecks, and why the web needed another major upgrade.

items.title: How to Scale an “AI App” to 1 Million Users in Production
items.author: Louis-François Bouchard
items.content:
Traditional software gets cheaper per user as it scales.

Yet AI software on an API does not!…

Every request runs a model, every model call has a per-token price, and the price stays “flat” whether ten people use it or a million do.

Self-hosting changes this, as GPU costs amortize across users.

But it introduces a new problem: capacity planning, hardware management, and a minimum spend that has to be justified before the first user arrives.

So scaling an AI product forces cost decisions most software never encounters, and most engineering teams face them only after users have already arrived.

Building an AI system that produces correct, grounded, and safe responses is one challenge…Serving those responses reliably and affordably to a million users is another.

This newsletter shows you how to redesign a chat assistant for large-scale production, reduce inference costs & build the infrastructure needed to handle millions of users.

Agents are killing your apps with compounding latency across workflows.

Your customers want their agent workflows to be efficient, so you’re losing deals if you don’t make them event-driven. Webhooks solve this issue, but implementing them is harder than it looks.

If you homebrewed your webhooks and are getting pinged at 4 in the morning for failed deliveries, this is for you.

handles everything: retries, idempotency, security, and compliance. Qualified startups get $12,000 in free credits.

(Thanks to for partnering on this newsletter.)

He’s a best-selling author (Building LLMs for Production), the co-founder of Towards AI, and the creator of the YouTube Channel, What’s AI, where he helps people understand AI and learn how to apply it in the real world. Through his development work with clients, content, teaching, AI training programs, and the new Mentorship program at Towards AI Academy, Louis focuses on making AI practical for builders, engineers, and curious learners alike.

At Towards AI, he and his team train AI engineers through courses and mentorship built for every stage, from beginner to advanced. That educational mission and the real-world experience building for his clients are exactly why I wanted him in this newsletter series.

Here’s what’s inside this newsletter:

  • Your $193,000 AI bill could drop to $48,000. Three optimizations cut the projected monthly cost by 75% at 100,000 daily conversations. Most teams overlook where the biggest savings actually come from.

  • Your smartest AI model could be your biggest money leak. Up to 70% of requests in our example go to a cheaper model, while the expensive one handles the rest. The surprising part is what happens to the total bill.

  • At 100K users, renting AI could beat owning GPUs. A $48,000 API bill competes with a $49,560 self-hosted setup. At 1 million daily conversations, the economics flip dramatically.

  • One GPU benchmark could wipe out $182,000 in monthly savings. Self-hosting looks 38% cheaper at scale, until lower throughput forces you to rent dozens of additional GPUs.

  • Your AI could pass every test and still break in production. The hidden gaps between evaluations, guardrails, and real user behavior, and why production failures need to become tests before the next release.

Should You Plan for a Million Users?

For most AI products, planning for a million users too early wastes time & money.

An API key and a credit card are often enough to launch a prototype. You should focus on building a useful product before investing in complex infrastructure.

But as your user base grows, these challenges become HARD to ignore:

  • Cost increases with usage. A chat assistant costs approximately $0.064 per conversation using GPT-5.4.

    • At 100 daily users, the monthly model bill reaches roughly $193.

    • At 100,000 daily users, it grows to $193,000.

    • At one million, it reaches $1.93 million.

    Model routing & caching reduce the cost per conversation, but total spending still grows with usage.

  • Latency increases under heavy traffic. An AI system that responds in 400 milliseconds with ten concurrent users could take two seconds with a thousand. As incoming requests approach the system’s serving capacity, queues grow & response times increase.

  • Small prompt changes become expensive. Adding 200 tokens to your system prompt across one million daily requests produces six billion additional input tokens per month. At GPT-5.4’s input price of $2.50 per million tokens, that adds $15,000 to your monthly bill before prompt caching.

  • API rate limits restrict scalability. AI providers enforce limits on requests & tokens per minute. As traffic grows, these limits could prevent your application from serving more users, even when your infrastructure has spare capacity.

  • Unit economics determine profitability. If each conversation costs more than the revenue it generates, acquiring more users increases your losses. You need to measure cost per conversation against the revenue it produces.

These challenges determine when your AI application needs more advanced production infrastructure.

So before moving beyond a managed API, evaluate these four constraints:

  • Does the cost per successful conversation support your target profit margin?

  • Service level objectives (SLOs): Does the system meet your latency, availability, and reliability targets?

  • Does your provider support your expected request and token volume?

  • Does the provider meet your requirements for where user data gets processed & stored?

As long as your API provider meets these requirements, staying with managed infrastructure is often the “simplest” choice.

The rest of this newsletter shows you how to estimate costs, identify scalability bottlenecks, and decide when more advanced infrastructure becomes necessary.

Our goal is to scale an AI chat assistant to while keeping inference costs under control.

For simplicity, we assume each daily active user starts one conversation. Each conversation contains eight requests to the language model.

Let’s define the token usage for each request:

  • 1,024 tokens for the system prompt and a fixed few-shot examples. This meets OpenAI’s minimum prefix length for prompt caching.

  • 400 tokens for conversation history & current user message.

  • 300 billed tokens generated by the model.

Each request therefore processes 1,424 input tokens & generates 300 output tokens.

With eight requests per conversation, the total becomes:

  • 11,392 tokens per conversation.

  • 2,400 tokens per conversation.

(These are illustrative assumptions. In production, you should replace them with actual token usage collected from your application.)

Our production system must meet seven requirements:

  • Keep model costs below a budget of $0.02 per conversation. Determine your actual budget from revenue per successful conversation and required gross margin.

  • Define service level objectives () for each workload, including time to first token () for interactive chat & completion deadlines for asynchronous jobs.

  • Maintain 99.9% uptime, including during model & prompt updates.

  • Support model changes with a reliable rollback mechanism.

  • Record token usage, cost, latency & model information for each request.

  • Collect user feedback & incorporate reviewed examples into evaluation datasets.

  • Estimate the financial impact of every change before deployment.

We’ll make five major design decisions:

  1. Reduce model costs by 50% to 80% through model routing, semantic caching, and prompt optimization.

  2. Explore quantization, GPU utilization, and serving frameworks to determine when self-hosting makes financial and technical sense.

  3. Production infrastructure: Handle concurrent traffic, control overload, and deploy model updates without disrupting users.

  4. Use production feedback to improve evaluation datasets & model quality over time.

  5. Capacity and cost estimation: Calculate infrastructure requirements & monthly costs at 10,000, 100,000, and one million daily users.

We’ll start with cost engineering because the budget per request influences every infrastructure decision that follows…

Three Types of Token Costs

Every request to a language model creates costs based on token usage.

For this example, we’ll focus on three types:

  • Tokens you send to the model, including the system prompt, conversation history, and user message, without a cached-input discount.

  • Previously processed input prefixes that the provider reuses at a discounted rate.

  • Tokens the model generates, including any billable reasoning tokens.

Output tokens typically cost more than input tokens because generating tokens one at a time (decode) has lower throughput than processing input tokens in parallel (prefill).

Some providers charge separately for extra features:

  • Anthropic charges approximately 1.25 to 2 times the standard input rate to create a cache entry, depending on its duration. Cache reads cost approximately 10% of the standard input rate.

  • Certain tools or external services introduce extra charges.

  • Higher-priority inference tiers could have different pricing.

  • Regional processing requirements could affect the final bill.

So check your provider’s billing structure before estimating production costs.

For the two OpenAI models below, output tokens cost as much as uncached input tokens.

These prices are a historical snapshot… Model availability & pricing change over time, so verify the latest rates before making deployment decisions.

Next, let’s use these token prices to calculate the monthly cost of serving thousands/millions of conversations.

Estimate costs before building the system.

Start with requests per day, estimate input, output, and cached-input tokens per request, then apply their respective rates. Multiply the daily cost by the number of days to get the monthly bill.

The arithmetic is straightforward…The challenge is accounting for every cost.

Retries & failed calls increase usage.

Agent loops multiply model calls per task. Embeddings and reranking add separate costs. Image and video processing introduce media-specific charges.

Semantic caching adds infrastructure costs, while provider-side prompt caching may introduce cache-write charges. Storage, network egress, observability, and idle GPU capacity when self-hosting also contribute to the total.

Even a complete cost estimate does not tell you whether the system produces useful answers. Track cost per successful task alongside total spending to measure .

Cost per successful task measures total spending divided by the number of tasks completed successfully.

Track it alongside quality and latency to understand the actual cost of delivering useful results. For example, suppose each conversation costs $0.064 on average. If 10% of conversations fail, the cost per successful conversation increases to approximately $0.071, assuming the average cost already includes failed attempts and retries.

The same principle applies to self-hosted models. Estimate the required token throughput, translate it into GPU capacity & calculate infrastructure costs.

H100 GPU rentals may cost around $2 to $6 per GPU-hour, depending on the provider, region, and rental terms. Newer Blackwell-class accelerators may have higher hourly rental prices.

But GPU rental prices alone do not determine inference cost:

Utilization, batching efficiency, memory requirements & model quality also affect the cost per successful task.

Faster or Cheaper, and When You Get Both

Latency & cost typically involve tradeoffs.

More powerful GPUs and lower batching levels reduce response times but increase cost per request.

Some optimizations improve both.

Smaller models require fewer resources, while shorter prompts reduce input processing. Prompt caching, quantization, and efficient attention kernels also reduce latency and cost, depending on the workload.

Streaming lets users see the response as it’s generated.

This improves perceived responsiveness without necessarily reducing total computation. Measure time to first token (), total response time & stream reliability separately.

Batching improves GPU utilization by processing multiple requests together.

Yet excessive batching can increase tail latency (p99). So interactive applications need different batching configurations from background workloads.

For tasks that do not require immediate responses, consider a provider’s Batch API. These asynchronous endpoints process requests within a specified window at a lower price.

OpenAI’s Batch API offers a 50% discount on supported workloads with a 24-hour completion window. Other providers have different pricing and processing limits.

Reasoning-Token Line Item

Some reasoning models generate internal reasoning tokens that users never see.

These tokens count toward output usage & get billed at output token rates.

This increases costs when switching models. Different models use different default reasoning-effort settings. If you leave the setting unspecified, a model upgrade could generate more reasoning tokens and increase the bill, even when the visible response stays the same.

Set reasoning effort explicitly where supported.

Track reasoning-token usage and total output costs for each request. Increase reasoning effort only when evaluations show enough improvement in answer quality to justify the extra cost.

The Anchor: 100K Conversations a Day

Picture an AI assistant handling 100,000 conversations per day, with eight model requests per conversation.

Each request uses 1,424 input tokens and 300 billed output tokens.

Over 30 days, the system processes 34.176 billion input tokens and 7.2 billion output tokens.

At GPT-5.4 rates of $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, the monthly cost is:

  • Total: $193,440 or $0.064 per conversation.

Suppose 70% of requests use GPT-5.4-mini, which costs $0.75 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens.

Assuming identical token usage across both models, routing reduces the monthly bill to approximately $98,635, a 49% reduction.

Plus, adding semantic caching, provider-side prompt caching, and shorter prompts could further reduce costs. Under a scenario with a 30% semantic-cache hit rate and additional prompt optimizations, the monthly bill could approach $48,000.

That represents approximately 75% savings compared with the original system.

Actual savings depend on traffic patterns, cache hit rates, token usage & model quality. Validate these assumptions against production measurements before relying on the estimate.

Model routing sends simpler requests to a cheaper model & complex requests to a more capable model.

A lightweight classifier or a smaller language model could decide which model should handle each request.

At scale, this significantly reduces inference costs. For example, routing 70% of requests to a cheaper model could lower the monthly bill. But the actual split depends on your workload and should come from production traffic & evaluation results.

The biggest risk is routing a complex request to a model that cannot handle it reliably. The smaller model may produce a confident but incorrect answer, reducing quality without an obvious failure.

To prevent this, evaluate the route system against the original system using a representative test dataset. Measure task success, factual accuracy, relevance, and other application-specific metrics.

The router should reduce costs while keeping quality within predefined acceptance thresholds. Track routing accuracy and cost per successful task to verify that the savings are worthwhile.

Model routing reduces costs by sending simpler requests to cheaper models.

Semantic caching goes further by reusing previously generated answers for similar questions, thus avoiding repeated model inference.

Semantic caching uses embeddings to find previously answered questions with similar meanings. If a cached answer passes the similarity and validity checks, the system returns it without calling the language model.

GPTCache is one open-source library for implementing this approach.

Cache effectiveness depends on traffic patterns. Frequently repeated questions, such as FAQs, produce higher hit rates, while unique or context-dependent queries benefit less.

Yet two failure modes require attention:

Two questions may have similar embeddings but require different answers.

Reusing an incorrect or outdated response silently reduces answer quality. Similarity thresholds, time-to-live () policies, and extra validation help reduce this risk.

2. Cross-user data leakage

Cache entries must be isolated by tenant & authorization scope.

Cache validity should account for relevant prompt, model, and retrieval-index versions, along with data freshness requirements. Authorization checks must remain enforced even when a cached answer exists.

Personalized responses should only be cached within properly isolated scopes.

Requests that perform actions or modify data must execute the required operations rather than replay a cached response.

Finally, semantic caching has its own costs, including embedding generation, vector search, and cache storage. So measure cache hit rate, false-hit rate, latency, and net cost savings to determine whether it improves the system.

The system prompt gets included in every model request.

So its length directly affects input-token usage and cost. In our example, the static prefix accounts for nearly three-quarters of each request’s input tokens.

Shortening instructions and removing unnecessary few-shot examples reduce token usage. But the actual savings depend on how much of the prompt already benefits from caching. Plus, removing important instructions reduces answer quality, so evaluate every change before deployment.

Prompt caching introduces another consideration:

Providers reuse previously processed input when requests share an identical token prefix. To maximize cache hits, place reusable instructions and examples first, followed by dynamic content such as user questions and retrieved documents.

For OpenAI’s automatic prompt caching, eligible prompts must contain at least 1,024 tokens. Shortening a reusable prefix below this threshold eliminates its caching benefit and potentially increases costs, even when the prompt becomes shorter.

In our cost example, we retain the 1,024-token static prefix and optimize the dynamic portion instead. This preserves the opportunity for prompt-cache savings while reducing unnecessary input tokens.

The goal is to minimize total input cost without sacrificing response quality.

Compare cached-token usage, total spending, and evaluation results before deciding which prompt version performs best.

When Smaller Models Are Good Enough

Smaller models significantly reduce inference costs, but only if they maintain acceptable answer quality.

Evaluate each candidate model against a representative test dataset that includes common requests, complex queries, and edge cases. Measure task success, factual accuracy, relevance, and other application-specific metrics.

If the smaller model meets predefined quality thresholds, it passes the quality gate. Before deployment, it must also satisfy latency, reliability, security & rollback requirements.

Use evaluation results to decide when a smaller model is sufficient rather than relying on model size or benchmark rankings alone.

Model routing reduces average inference costs by selecting cheaper models, while semantic caching avoids repeated model calls.

The next step is optimizing the inference stack itself to reduce the computational cost of generating each token…

items.title: 64 AI Concepts Every Software Engineer Should Know
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
You ask an AI assistant a question…

But what actually happened between your question & the answer?

Behind that simple interaction sits a stack of models, tokens, context, retrieval, tools, evaluations, and infrastructure.

These 64 concepts will help you understand how modern AI systems actually work, from the neural networks underneath them to agents & applications built on top.

Curious to know how many were new to you:

  1. Retrieval augmented generation,

  2. AI agents & agentic workflows,

  3. Transformers and self-attention,

  4. Model evaluation and evaluation-driven development,

  5. Fine tuning and instruction tuning,

  6. Reasoning & chain-of-thought.

( …and much more in Parts 2, 3 & 4!)

  • What it means and how it works,

  • A real-world analogy where useful,

  • A common mistake to avoid,

Agents are killing your apps with compounding latency across workflows.

Your customers want their agent workflows to be efficient, so you’re losing deals if you don’t make them event-driven. Webhooks solve this issue, but implementing them is harder than it looks.

If you homebrewed your webhooks and are getting pinged at 4 in the morning for failed deliveries, this is for you.

handles everything: retries, idempotency, security, and compliance. Qualified startups get $12,000 in free credits.

A large language model () is an AI model trained on vast amounts of text to learn language patterns.

You type into a chatbot & hit Enter.

The model processes your question as small pieces of text called . A token could be a word, part of a word, or punctuation. A typical text-generating LLM selects the next token based on your question and the text it has produced so far.

Then it repeats. Token by token, the answer appears…

During training, the model adjusted internal numerical values called . Those weights capture patterns useful for language tasks, from sentence structure to relationships between ideas.

Your prompt gives the model context for its response.

Think of autocomplete on your phone:

You type and the keyboard suggests “.” An LLM takes this idea much further, using the available conversation to produce paragraphs, explanations, or code.

Predicting a plausible continuation still leaves room for a wrong answer.

Trusting an answer simply because it sounds .

Suppose you ask for code to resize an image. The model could suggest a function with a sensible name that the library doesn’t provide. Check the documentation & run the code before you rely on it.

You don’t need a separate model for every language task.

Different instructions let the same LLM summarize a document, explain an error, or draft a reply.

That flexibility makes LLMs useful across many software products.

Generative AI produces content such as text, images, audio & video from patterns learned during training.

Ask an image generator for “a red bicycle outside a bakery.”

Your description guides the model toward a result. Some image models begin with random noise and refine it step by step into an image. A text model uses a different process, typically selecting tokens in sequence.

Both produce content from learned patterns.

Generative AI is the broader category… Text-generating LLMs are one example; image and audio generators are others.

Think of a cook who has learned from hundreds of recipes:

You ask for a spicy vegetable dish. The cook draws on familiar ingredients and techniques to prepare something that fits your request.

You still taste the dish before you serve it.

Assuming the generated content is ready to use.

An image could contain unreadable labels. A summary could leave out a key decision. Review the result against your original request and check factual details against the source.

Generative AI helps you get from a blank page to a first draft.

A few notes become an email, a description becomes an illustration, or a specification becomes starter code.

The next step is to check whether the draft does the job.

Machine Learning () is a branch of AI in which systems learn from data to perform tasks without explicit rules for every situation.

Think about the spam folder in your inbox:

You could write a rule to block every email containing But a spammer could change the wording; also, a legitimate email could contain the same phrase. A model learns from examples & considers several clues together.

Those clues help it assess a new message.

For a spam filter, training examples typically include the correct label:. The training algorithm adjusts the model to reduce classification errors.

This approach is called .

Other approaches discover patterns in unlabeled data or learn through rewards after actions.

Think about how you learn to choose ripe fruit:

Someone shows you a few good examples & a few bad ones. Over time, you connect color, firmness, and smell with ripeness.

You use those clues on your next trip to the market.

Testing the model with the same examples it learned from.

That’s like giving a student the practice questions again and calling it a final exam. Reserve separate examples to check whether the model handles unfamiliar data.

ML helps when a task involves more patterns than you could reasonably capture in hand-written rules. It powers uses such as spam filters, fraud detection, and product recommendations.

The goal is useful predictions on new data.

Deep learning () is a type of ML that uses multiple layers of a neural network to learn complex patterns.

Show a model a photograph of a bicycle.

The model receives numbers representing the image’s pixels. Early layers often detect simple features, such as edges & textures. Later layers combine these features into more complex shapes & object parts.

Together, the layers help the model recognize the bicycle.

The word “deep” refers to these multiple layers. During training, the model adjusts them to improve its predictions.

Think of a sketch as someone draws it:

First, you see a few lines and circles. Add a frame, handlebars, and pedals, and the shapes start to make sense together.

A deep network also combines simpler features into more complex patterns.

Assuming every problem needs deep learning.

For a small spreadsheet of house sizes and prices, a simpler model could do the job well. Test a basic approach first, then compare whether a deep network earns its extra cost and complexity.

Images, speech & language contain patterns which are difficult to describe with fixed rules. Deep learning helps models learn useful features from these inputs.

It underpins tools such as speech recognition & image classification.

A neural network is a model made of connected mathematical units that transform inputs into an output.

Let’s look inside the layers we just discussed:

Each unit receives numbers, combines them, and passes a result onward. Connections have adjustable values called weights, which control how much each input contributes. Layers also apply transformations, so the network learns more complex relationships.

The final layer produces the model’s output.

During training, an error measure tells the system how far its predictions are from the target. The training algorithm uses this feedback to adjust weights and other values across the network.

Tiny adjustments, repeated across many examples, change its predictions.

Think of the controls on a sound mixing desk:

One control increases the voice; another reduces the drums. Changing the controls changes the final sound.

Weights play a similar role in how a network combines its inputs.

Taking the word “neural” too literally.

The name draws inspiration from the brain, but these units perform mathematical operations. A network’s ability to recognize a face or produce a sentence doesn’t establish human-like thought.

Neural networks provide the structure behind deep learning.

Understanding weights also explains what training changes: numerical values a model uses to turn an input into a prediction.

6. Retrieval-Augmented Generation

RAG is an approach that retrieves relevant information & supplies it to a model to help generate an answer.

Ask a company assistant, “How long do I have to return this order?”

The application searches the company’s documents for the relevant return policy. It places matching passages alongside your question. The model uses those passages to write its response.

The answer has information from the company’s documents.

Updating those documents gives the application new material to retrieve. It doesn’t require a new training run for every policy change.

Think of an open-book exam:

You find the relevant pages before you answer. Your result depends on both finding the right material & interpreting it correctly.

Assuming retrieval guarantees a correct answer.

The search could return an outdated policy and/or miss an exception. So check the retrieved passages & final response. When the evidence is missing, the assistant should say so.

RAG helps assistants answer questions about private or frequently updated information. Also it gives readers source material to check against the answer.

7. AI Agents and Agentic Workflows

An AI agent uses a model to choose actions toward a goal and respond to the results. Agentic workflows organize model and tool steps into a process.

Ask an assistant to investigate a failed software test.

An agent would inspect the error, open a file, make an edit, and rerun the tests. The result helps it decide what to do next. A fixed workflow follows a prewritten sequence, such as “summarize the ticket, classify it, then route it.”

The difference is how much control the model has over the next step.

The term “agentic workflow” covers a range of designs. Some follow mostly fixed steps; others give the model more freedom to choose.

Think of a technician with a checklist:

For a routine inspection, the checklist determines the order. For an unfamiliar fault, the technician chooses the next check based on what the previous one revealed.

Giving an agent tools without clear limits.

A failed action could trigger repeated retries/unwanted changes. So set permissions, spending limits, and stopping conditions. Plus, require approval before consequential actions, such as a payment/deletion.

Agents help with tasks whose steps depend on discoveries along the way.

Fixed workflows work when the sequence is known and predictable execution matters.

items.title: API design was HARD until I learned these 33 concepts
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
No time for small talk today:

The following is the second of a premium 2-part newsletter... if you’re serious about API design in 2026, then this newsletter is for YOU.

On with part 2 of the newsletter:

Some of these API design concepts are , and some are . ALL of them are super useful to software engineers building scalable APIs.

Curious to know how many were new to you:

    • What it is & how it works (in plain English),

    • A real-world analogy (if I found one),

    Agents can generate code. Getting it right for your system, team conventions, and past decisions is the hard part. You end up wasting time and tokens in correction loops.

    More MCPs give agents access to information but not understanding. The teams pulling ahead use a context layer to give agents exactly what they need.

    • Where teams get stuck on the AI maturity curve

    • How a context layer solves for quality, efficiency, and cost

    • Live demo: the same coding task with and without a context layer

    (Thanks to Unblocked for partnering on this newsletter.)

    JSON Web Token () is a signed token that contains claims about the caller.

    Three parts, separated by dots.

    • names the algorithm.

    • holds the claims: this is user 42, they expire at noon, and have the admin role.

    • proves nobody altered the first two parts. The server verifies signature with a key it already holds, reads the claims, and answers the request without touching a session store.

    The token carries its own proof, so verification costs no database call.

    It says which zones you may enter and which day it dies. Security reads it in a glance without radioing the ticket office. If you tamper with it, the seal breaks, so the guard knows.

    You cannot easily revoke a token.

    Fire an employee at nine, and their token still opens doors until it expires. The payload is signed, not encrypted, so anyone holding the token can read every claim inside it.

    So keep expiry short, keep secrets out of payload, and use a refresh token to renew.

    Stateless authentication across microservices, and the access token most OAuth providers hand back.

    Its structure is fixed by a public specification, which is why every language has a library for it. Pair it with Authentication, which is the job it exists to do.

    Throttling slows down a caller instead of turning them away.

    Rate limiting & throttling get used interchangeably, and they do different things.

    A rate limiter counts requests and rejects the ones over the cap with a . A throttle accepts the request and delays it. It queues the call, releases it when capacity frees up, or answers with a that asks the client to come back shortly. The work still happens, just later and more slowly.

    Rejection protects the server…Throttling protects the server & keeps the caller alive.

    A metered on-ramp to a motorway.

    The light drips cars onto the carriageway one at a time. Nobody is sent home. The queue on the ramp is annoying, and it's why the motorway itself keeps moving at seventy.

    A queued request holds a connection, and enough of them exhaust the very resource you were protecting.

    Plus, delay hides the problem, so a service that has been struggling for an hour looks merely sluggish. So cap the queue & alert on the delay rather than the errors.

    Expensive operations, shared infrastructure, and any burst you would rather absorb than reject.

    Envoy, Kong, and most message queues implement it. Pair it with rate limiting, and be explicit in your documentation about which one you are doing.

    An endpoint is a uniform resource locator () that points to one resource on your server.

    It’s the address you aim a request at.

    • is that user’s orders.

    The path names the resource & the method names the action; together, they define one operation. Get the path wrong, and you receive a rather than the data you meant to ask for.

    Read a good endpoint aloud, and it explains itself.

    The number and the road identify one door out of a million. Post a letter to the wrong number, and it arrives somewhere real, which is worse than it not arriving at all.

    Endpoint names drift as the API grows.

    One person writes , the next writes , and six months later your API reads like it was designed by a committee that never met.

    Use plural nouns for collections and let the verb live in the method.

    The first thing anybody learns about your API, and the thing they will curse if you got it wrong.

    Every REST framework routes on them. Pair it with OpenAPI, which turns your endpoint list into documentation nobody has to maintain by hand.

    The request-response cycle is the basic way clients & servers communicate. The client sends a request, and server returns a response.

    Every call follows the same simple script.

    A request names what you want and where: a method, a path, a few headers, a body when there is one to send. The server reads it, does the work, and answers with a status code and usually a body of its own. The exchange is synchronous, so the client holds the line open and waits for that single reply before it does anything else.

    Send, wait, read the reply. That is the entire cycle.

    Posting a letter and waiting by the mailbox.

    You write the address on the envelope, the details inside, and a return address on the back. Then you stand there. Nothing else happens until the reply lands.

    The client blocks and a slow server holds that connection, and work that takes two minutes leaves a user staring at a spinner. Nothing comes back until everything comes back.

    Accept the request, return a , and finish the work in the background.

    The foundation under REST, GraphQL, and almost every API you will build.

    Its rules are set by the HTTP specification. Pair it with Webhooks and WebSockets, the two answers for when waiting is the wrong shape.

    Want life to feel a little easier?

    Ben Meer’s new book, , is packed with practical systems for work, health, money, relationships, home, and more.

    Headers are key-value pairs that carry information about a request/response, separate from the body.

    They describe the message rather than contain it.

    • says what format the body is in.

    • carries the credential.

    • tells every cache along the path how long to keep a copy.

    • states what the client can understand.

    • names the software that called.

    Servers, proxies, and browsers all read them before touching the body.

    Metadata belongs on the outside.

    The outside of an envelope.

    Stamps, postcodes, fragile stickers, return address. Every courier along the route reads the outside and acts on it. None of them open the letter.

    Headers are easy to forget, which is why so many bugs end in a nobody set.

    Sizes are capped, casing rules surprise people, and a header stripped by a proxy fails silently rather than loudly. So log the headers you rely on, and set explicitly every time.

    Authentication, caching, versioning, compression, and cross-origin rules all ride on them.

    Any browser’s network tab shows you every one. Pair it with Caching, which does nothing at all unless the headers say so.

    OpenAPI is a standard file that describes every endpoint, parameter, and response of your API in one place.

    You write it in YAML/JSON, and machines read it.

    From that one file, you generate interactive documentation, client libraries in eight languages, a mock server for the front end to build against, and a test suite that catches the day your response shape quietly changed. The specification becomes the contract, and the contract becomes the source of truth.

    Write it once & stop maintaining documentation by hand.

    An architect’s blueprint.

    The plumber, electrician, and joiner all work from the same drawing without ever meeting. Change the drawing, and everyone sees the change. Change the wall without changing the drawing, and somebody drills through a pipe.

    A hand-written spec drifts from the code within weeks, and a spec that lies is worse than no spec at all. The file grows long, and reviewing a two-thousand-line YAML diff is nobody’s favorite afternoon.

    Generate the spec from your code, or test your code against the spec.

    Public APIs, partner integrations, and any backend whose consumers sit in a different room.

    Swagger UI, Redoc, and Stoplight render it. Pair it with API Versioning, since each version deserves its own contract.

    A timeout is the longest a caller will wait for a response before giving up.

    Without one, a caller waits forever.

    Set a connect timeout for reaching the server and a read timeout for hearing back. When a downstream service hangs, your request fails in two seconds instead of hanging alongside it. This matters because every waiting request holds a thread, a connection, and a slot in your pool. Enough of them & your healthy service falls over next to the sick one.

    A fast failure beats a slow hang.

    Hanging up after thirty seconds of ringing.

    Nobody is home. Listening to the ringtone for an hour won't make them answer, and it stops you from calling anybody else.

    Set one too tight, and you kill healthy requests that were simply slow; then you retry them, and you have doubled the load on a service that was only having a bad minute.

    Measure your ninety-ninth percentile, then set the timeout above it.

    Every network call you make is the first line of defense against a cascading failure.

    Every HTTP client has a default, and the default is usually wrong. Pair it with Circuit Breaker, which you reach for when timeouts stop being occasional.

    Microservices split one application into small, independent services that talk to each other over APIs.

    Each service owns one job and its own data.

    The service owns the orders table. The service owns payments. Neither reaches into the other’s database. They call each other’s APIs, deploy on their own schedule, and scale independently, so a search feature under load gets more servers without anybody touching checkout.

    Independence is the whole point, and the network is the whole cost.

    A food court instead of one enormous kitchen.

    Each unit runs its own stoves, staff, and menu. The pizza place closes for a refit, and everyone else keeps serving. Ordering a meal from three units means three queues.

    Every function call you used to make in memory is now a network call that can time out, arrive twice, or never arrive.

    A bug spans four services and six log files. Keeping data consistent across services is a hard problem with no free answer. So start with a monolith, and split it when the pain is real, not theoretical.

    Large systems, large organizations, and any codebase where two changes cannot ship without waiting for each other.

    The patterns that make it survivable deserve an article of their own. Pair it with API Gateway and gRPC, which keep the pieces reachable and fast.

    • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

    • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability, and performance.
